learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparison of numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Committed Almost never under 1 in 100 for the explicitly described lead-of-two copying rule, 100 people and two-thirds reliable clues.
observations.exploration: Ran 1 then 100 then 10000, totaling 10101 crowds: 2009 wrong, 19.9%, versus pooled clues 2 wrong, 0.02%. Last run had 62 blue clues but 1 blue pick; toggling views exposed 61 people opposing their clues. Reliability changes reset run counters: 60% gave 30.9% wrong versus pooled 1.63%; 80% gave 5.9% versus pooled zero over 10000 runs.
observations.reveal: Corrected prediction to about one in five, exact 20%. Explained lead-of-two absorption, including wrong leads after split starts. Distinguished single-person error 33.3% from cascade and pooled errors. Reveal retains original two-thirds run snapshot while stage notes identify later parameter values.
observations.visual: Actual dark 1257 by 936 screenshots inspected. Blue circles/red squares encode colours with shape; rings mark first lead of two and outlines mark picks against clues. Pooled view replaces almost all-red choices with majority-blue signals. Dense dot field but readable legend and counters.
observations.previewIsolation: Preview banner excluded history and analytics saves.
observations.blinding: No source, metadata or other reviewer judgments inspected.

prediction.reason: Explicit rule and concrete error choices support a meaningful commitment.
prediction.evidence: Lead-of-two copying and clue accuracy provided.

interaction.reason: Batch runs, pooled comparison and reliability parameters expose information loss.
interaction.evidence: Same run: 62 blue clues but 1 blue pick; 60% and 80% contrasts tested.

payoff.reason: Reveal explains why many copied actions are not independent evidence.
payoff.evidence: Ring marks absorbing lead; split starts can also reach wrong lead.

clarity.reason: Shapes, outlines and explicit rates make the mechanism legible.
clarity.evidence: Original run snapshot and current stage notes label their clue accuracy separately.

transfer.reason: General crowd-information principle without a new application task.
transfer.evidence: Only toy urn rule and reliability variants offered.

accessibility.evidence: Visual shapes and ordinary clicks inspected; assistive modes untested.

surprise.reason: A nearly unanimous wrong crowd hides a majority of correct private signals.

visualExplanation.reason: Same-run toggle directly reveals evidence discarded by copying.
visualExplanation.evidence: Outlined dissenting clues and lead-of-two ring.

playfulness.reason: Fast simulations and reversible evidence views invite comparison.
playfulness.evidence: One, hundred, ten-thousand runs plus accuracy controls.

practicalValue.reason: Useful distinction between copied choices and independent information.
practicalValue.evidence: Pooled evidence strongly outperforms copying in the stated rule.

depth.reason: Links individual reliability, stopping event and aggregate failure.
depth.evidence: Exact 20% differs from two immediate wrong clues at 11.1%.

complexity.reason: Simulation supports a probabilistic mechanism without requiring a derivation.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Separate choices from signals and recognize dependence after a lead.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Three batch controls, three accuracy options and one view toggle.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: A hundred symbols, outlines, ring and percentage counters.

whyCool: A single toggle reveals that apparent consensus can conceal contrary private evidence.
caveat: Fixed toy copying rule; no fresh real-world application or independence audit.
effort: Approximately 3 minutes of actual browser review.
